weakness: The program measured both objects once at the start and grasped the second object several seconds later from that stale measurement. When the box was nudged 8 cm during the first grasp, the second grasp closed on empty air and the program gave up (0/10).
how_found: I questioned the assumption that objects stay where they were first measured until the arm reaches them. I suspected it because the second grasp starts about 4 s after the only measurement, and a real scene can be bumped in that time.
why_missed: In the base task nothing moves, so one measurement at t=0 is as good as a fresh one. Averaging eight detections made the stale estimate look precise, which hid that it could be out of date.
fix: Each object is now re-measured right before it is grasped, once two looks 0.3 s apart agree (it is at rest). After closing, the program checks that the fingers closed on something without being wedged open, and that the object rose with the lift; otherwise it retries with another grasp point. While recovering, the base task exposed two more fragile steps. (1) The scan pose is now computed from fresh measurements of both held objects instead of one open-loop placement. The free roll about the scan axis is chosen to keep the wrist near its start orientation, because the planner had reported success for a pose where the wrist folded into its own arm. (2) Every move is checked against the commanded pose.
general_rule: Act on a measurement taken right before the action, not one from the start: re-perceive an object when you are about to touch it, after it has come to rest, and afterwards confirm the action had its intended effect (object in hand, object lifted, arm actually at the commanded pose).

weakness: The box was always brought to one fixed meeting point in front of the robot, and the scanner was sent there without telling the planner about anything else on the table. A pole standing at that spot blocked half of the scans (5/10 failed).
how_found: I questioned the hard-coded meeting point: the program never looks at whether the space where the two hands meet is free. Real tables often have something standing in the middle.
why_missed: The base scene is empty above the table, so a constant meeting point always worked. I had copied the scripted expert's fixed target pose without asking where it came from.
fix: Candidate meeting points are now tested against the perceived obstacles, with the needed space sized from the measured box and scanner, and every move gives the obstacles to the planner. Moving the meeting point closer to the robot then folded the box arm's wrist into its own links while the planner still reported success. So the presentation now uses the box's free roll about its scan axis to keep the hand near its start orientation, checks that the arm arrived, and otherwise tries the next roll, then the next meeting point. The box's target orientation is defined by its scan-face direction, not by a fixed quaternion that the placement helper had never actually enforced.
general_rule: Never hard-code where an action happens: choose the spot from perceived free space sized from the measured objects, give the planner every obstacle, use any free degree of freedom of the goal (such as a roll that does not matter) to keep the arm in a natural posture, and confirm the arm actually arrived before continuing.

weakness: The arms were assigned from the scanner's side alone, and the box went to the other arm wherever it was. With both objects on the left (scanner near the middle, box far left), the right arm reached across the table for the box and failed (1/10).
how_found: I questioned the assumption that the two objects lie on opposite sides of the robot. Nothing in a real scene guarantees that, and the program never looks at where the second object is before committing an arm to it.
why_missed: The task's own randomisation always puts the objects on opposite sides, and the scripted expert decides from one object's side. I copied that rule without asking whether the layout could differ.
fix: Arms are now assigned jointly: for each of the two assignments, check that each object has a reachable grasp for its arm, and pick the feasible one with the least total sideways reach. Recovering also exposed two latent bugs in the scan loop. (1) Re-aiming searched only the four best-ranked rolls, so the chosen roll could drop out of the list and no correction happened. (2) Once corrections did happen, a tolerance tighter than the measurement noise triggered needless re-planned moves; one of them folded the wrist and knocked the scanner out of the hand. The final check now averages 20 detections and accepts within 1.2 cm (success allows 2.5 cm). Corrections are small straight-line moves instead of re-plans, and free meeting points away from the body are preferred over ones close to it.
general_rule: Decide which arm handles which object from where all objects actually are and whether each arm can reach its object, never from the position of one object alone.

rejected_before: v5 (validity: clutter generator adds a ground body)
weakness: After the first arm picked its object, it parked right above where the other arm had to reach. Each arm's planner knows nothing about the other arm, so with the box set down right in front of the scanner the second arm's wrist ran into the first arm's fingers (7/10 failed).
how_found: I questioned the assumption that the arm that has finished its pick never stands in the other arm's way. That holds only because the task normally puts the objects on opposite sides, and the planner models one arm at a time.
why_missed: The base layout keeps the two arms' workspaces apart, so a resting pose 'lifted above where I grasped' never got in the way of anything.
fix: After the first pick, the busy hand moves at least 25 cm (horizontally) away from the second object and up. If that move cannot be planned it tries alternatives: away from the object, back towards its own side, then straight up. The second arm's planner is given the object in the busy hand as an obstacle. Making the box an obstacle for the scanner grasp was tried and reverted: the inflated box blocked the scanner's only grasp approach.
general_rule: In two-arm work, treat the other arm and whatever it holds as an obstacle: before one arm works somewhere, move the other arm clear of that area, because each arm's planner does not know about the other.

weakness: With the box at the back edge of the arms' reach, four things went wrong. (1) The straight-line top-down approach could not be planned. (2) A lift that could not be planned was treated as a failed grasp, so the program opened the hand and dropped a box it was holding. (3) A side grasp's approach pushed the box off the table. (4) Carrying the box back and aiming the scanner from those far postures folded the wrists into the arm, which the planner does not model.
how_found: I questioned the assumption that every grasp, lift and carry is comfortably inside the arms' reach. A box put down at the back of the table is common, and the program had never been near the reach limit.
why_missed: All objects in the task start in a band near the robot, so no motion was ever close to the reach limit, and a planning failure had always meant 'blocked', never 'too far'.
fix: Six repairs: (1) alternative lifts that pull the object towards the body; (2) more grasp attempts; (3) when the straight approach cannot be planned, grasp 2 cm higher from a short approach; (4) that approach kept straight and verified (an unconstrained plan for a 1 cm move swung the whole arm into the robot's body); (5) returning to the start pose after a try that did not arrive (it helped here but made the close-together layout worse, 0.9 to 0.5); (6) dropping hand poses below table clearance. The best state reached v9 0.9 with another scene at 0.5, and the last 0.6. Unsolved; the pipeline was reverted to round 4.
general_rule: A motion that cannot be planned leaves the world unchanged: never undo progress (release a held object, abandon a grasp) because the planner said no; first try other motions that stay inside the reachable workspace, such as pulling the object towards the body.

weakness: When a tall object filled the whole usual meeting area, every spot on the short meeting list was blocked, and the program fell back to the default spot, which it knew to be blocked (0/10). Recovering also showed that grasps of objects a few cm from a tall obstacle are caught between two planner limits. With the obstacle in the planner's world, its coarse hand model refuses the straight approach; without it, the wrist really does hit the obstacle.
how_found: I questioned the assumption that some spot on the short list of meeting points is free, and that the default spot will do if none is.
why_missed: Round 2 replaced the fixed spot with a short list of alternatives and kept a fallback to the default. With one thin obstacle there was always a free entry, so the fallback was never exercised.
fix: Six repairs: (1) a grid of meeting points searched nearest-first, never falling back to a known-blocked spot (0.0 to 0.3); (2-3) giving a grasp and its lift only the obstacles near the object (0.3 to 0.6); (4) ranking height before depth for meeting points (0.8, but the close-together layout fell to 0.7); (5) always giving the planner what the other hand holds (all older scenes 0.8-1.0, v10 0.7); (6) a short-approach grasp fallback (v10 0.7, close-together layout 0.6). Unsolved; the pipeline was reverted to round 4.
general_rule: When the usual places are all blocked, search a wider space that is actually free (higher, further) instead of falling back to a default you already know is blocked; if nothing free is found, stop rather than act into a known collision.
